abstract: The vast majority of natural metabolic pathways remain uncharacterized, limiting the ability to harness biological systems for industrial biotechnology and environmental bioremediation. Classical functional genomics and activity-guided purification protocols frequently fail to map multi-step metabolic cascades due to transient protein-substrate interactions, rapid metabolic flux, and the inherent complexity of complex cellular proteomes. Here, I present the comprehensive protocol for Sequential Affinity-Based Pathway Mapping (SAMP) an iterative, multi-phase chromatographic framework designed to systematically trace metabolic cascades across different chemical states of matter (solid, liquid, and gas). By utilizing the native or immobilized state of a metabolic substrate as an affinity bait for cellular proteomes, SAMP enables the layer-by-layer isolation, elution, and structural characterization of sequential enzymes within an uncharacterized cascade. I highlight the utility of this method using bacterial plastic degradation as an archetypal model for solid-phase systems, detail the physical encapsulation frameworks required for unstable or liquid intermediates, and propose a pressurized micro-perfusion strategy to handle volatile gaseous substrates.
